title: Embeddings & Rerank — vector dims, batch sizing, latency SLOs (hybrid deploy deep dive)
summary: Deep dive on embeddings + rerank architecture for user-facing search: comparing 1024 vs 768 dims, batching strategies, kv/prefix caching benefits, mixed-precision quantization tradeoffs, and hybrid routing (hosted + private VPC). Agreed to run a 2-week pilot measuring p99 latency and cost per 1M queries with three configs; Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet and security docs.
topics: batch size and its impact on p50/p95/p99 latency
KV cache / prefix caching for rerank workflows
hybrid routing: hosted fallback vs private VPC on-prem
cost math: $/1M queries and GPU utilization assumptions
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-03 15:00 PST | Duration: 56m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Dovetail), Luca Marino, Samir Patel

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, sorry for the slight delay, we had a quick sync on another call. Recording started.
00:22 Priya Nair: No worries. Quick context, we run a rerank pipeline where we generate embeddings server side and then do a similarity rerank. Our latency SLO for the UX is 120ms p95, ideally 80ms p50. We're trying to get cost under control as traffic scales.
00:41 Ethan Park: Got it. Today we'd like to walk through three configs we usually benchmark: a higher-dim 1024 embedding baseline, a lower-dim 768 model with optimized kernel selection, and a quantized 8/4-bit variant. We'll cover batching, KV cache for prefix reuse, and where hybrid routing helps.
01:05 Luca Marino: Quick Q — we're on a VPC now for data locality, so private deployment is required for the pilot, but we want hosted fallback for burst. Is that a supported pattern?
01:18 Maya Chen: Yes, hybrid routing is supported — you can route by policy: private first, then hosted as failover or for burst. There are a couple of notes about data residency and audit logs; we'll include those in the security packet.
01:31 Samir Patel: Cool. Show us some numbers though — like p99 implications when you increase batch sizes.
01:38 Ethan Park: Sure, I'll share the rough numbers from our internal microbenchmarks. These are indicative: Baseline 1024 unquantized on A10G-type = p50 25ms token, p95 90ms, p99 210ms for full rerank flow at batch 8. Moving to 768 dims with the same model family reduces compute about ~30% so p50 18ms, p95 70ms, p99 140ms. When we enable a 8-bit quantized path we saw further compute drop, p50 12ms, p95 45ms, p99 90ms but you need to validate accuracy.
02:10 Priya Nair: Those p99 numbers look high for our SLO. Are those for the embedding generation only or end-to-end rerank?
02:18 Ethan Park: That's embedding generation and vector scoring together in the rerank loop — end-to-end per request. If you split the pipeline (embed once, cache the vector), the per-request cost for rerank falls dramatically.
02:29 Luca Marino: Can you explain more about the KV cache idea — we already do prefix caching for chat, is this similar?
02:36 Ethan Park: Similar concept. For rerank in search, the heavy part is model forward for generating embeddings. If many queries share prefixes or the same document set, we can keep embeddings in a KV-store in memory on the serving nodes and avoid recompute. Example: for a user session with incremental query refinement, 60% of tokens can be served from KV so effective latency and cost drop. But eviction policy and memory footprint depend on vector dims — 1024 vectors cost more RAM.
03:05 Samir Patel: What's the memory math? We have about 10M cached vectors potential.
03:12 Ethan Park: Approx numbers: 768 float32 vector ~3KB, 1024 float32 ~4KB. So 10M * 3KB ~30GB, 10M * 4KB ~40GB, that fits on reasonable node pools but if you quantize to 8-bit or 4-bit you can reduce to ~25% or ~12.5% of that size respectively. So quantization helps caching cost but impacts similarity fidelity.
03:45 Priya Nair: Fidelity is our big concern for rerank. We can't degrade MRR by more than 1.5%. How do you recommend validating quantization?
03:55 Ethan Park: We recommend an eval set — run A/B with a sample of production queries across candidate sets. Redwood's Optimize can run regression alerts tied to evals and flag if MRR delta exceeds threshold. For 8-bit often there's negligible MRR drop, 4-bit is riskier and sometimes requires small calibration steps (per-layer scaling). We'll include suggested test prompts in the spreadsheet.
04:20 Maya Chen: I'll flag that in the next steps.
04:24 Priya Nair: Back to batch sizing — what's the sweet spot for latency SLOs for us? We are spikey traffic but want to keep cost low.
:04:33 Ethan Park: There's a trade: larger batches increase throughput and amortize dispatch overhead but also increase tail latency because you wait to fill a batch. For your 120ms p95 target if requests are bursty, we recommend small batch sizes (4-8) with dynamic batch timeout 10-20ms. For steady streams you can push batch 16-32 and hit better cost per token.
05:00 Luca Marino: Do you auto-tune batch timeouts?
05:03 Ethan Park: Redwood runtime supports workload-aware batching and you can set service-level policies per route. One mode is latency-first — it doesn't wait to fill batches beyond TTL; another is cost-first which will wait up to X ms. You can also pin certain routes to dedicated pools for predictable p99.
05:20 Samir Patel: Dedicated pools cost more though — what's the typical uplift?
05:25 Maya Chen: Dedicated capacity typically has a fixed monthly commitment plus lower variable cost for tokens. For our estimates, dependent on GPU type, you'd look at 20-40% higher committed cost but ~30-50% lower per-token in steady state for heavy throughput. We'll put exact math in the spreadsheet for your traffic profile.
05:42 Priya Nair: On hybrid — if we run private in our VPC and failover to hosted, what's the path for data that fails to meet residency?
05:50 Maya Chen: We can route only metadata/requests without PII to hosted fallback. For requests that must stay in VPC, Redwood allows a strict policy — no fallback. If you need burst to hosted we offer a masked/fuzzed payload option but that's case-by-case and needs compliance sign-off. We'll include compliance notes in the security packet.
06:12 Luca Marino: Okay. Can you walk through the pilot you'd recommend?
06:16 Ethan Park: Suggested pilot: 2-week run with three arms wired into production traffic sampling 1% each: (A) 1024 float32 baseline, batch=8, private nodes only; (B) 768 float32 optimized kernels, batch=8, private nodes + hosted fallback; (C) 768 with 8-bit quant (mixed precision), batch auto-tune. Measure: p50/p95/p99, MRR lift/delta, cost per 1M queries. We'll provide a turnkey benchmarking harness and the spreadsheet.
06:46 Priya Nair: Sounds good. How about expected dollars? Ballpark for cost per 1M queries?
06:52 Ethan Park: Ballpark: baseline 1024 float32 maybe $420-$480 per 1M queries depending on concurrency and eviction; 768 float32 could be $290-$340 per 1M; 768 + 8-bit quant ~$180-$240 per 1M. These are illustrative; exact depends on batch efficiency and KV hit rate.
07:14 Samir Patel: Those ranges are big — what assumptions drive the delta?
07:18 Ethan Park: Main factors: KV cache hit rate (if hit rate is high you save forward passes), batch fill efficiency (if your traffic allows big batches you save), and model kernel efficiency on the GPU (certain sequence lengths and dims map better to optimized kernels). Also network overhead for private VPC can add ms.
07:38 Priya Nair: Sequence length — our queries average 28 tokens. How does that affect kernel selection?
07:44 Ethan Park: Short sequences play well with attention-optimized kernels; for 28 tokens the runtime will pick kernels optimized for low-latency. Longer sequences increase memory and can reduce throughput. We'll share per-model perf profiles in the deck.
07:58 Maya Chen: I'm dropping links in chat: deck (redwood.com/decks/dovetail-emb-bench-v1.pdf) and the benchmark spreadsheet (redwood.com/spreadsheets/dovetail-bench-v1.xlsx).
08:12 Priya Nair: Noted. A few technical nitpicks: we use Faiss for nearest neighbor currently, if we move to an indexless rerank can Redwood integrate with our index or would we push vectors into your in-memory index?
08:24 Ethan Park: We support both: you can keep Faiss and call Redwood's embedding API and store vectors in your index, or you can push vectors into Redwood Dedicated's in-memory vector store for lower latency. For private on-prem we can run a co-located index service. Tradeoffs are control vs latency.
08:46 Luca Marino: Does dedicated in-memory store give deterministic p99?
08:50 Ethan Park: More deterministic yes, because you control the pool. But you still need to size for hot shards and budget cache eviction. We recommend sticky sharding for user sessions to keep locality.
09:04 Samir Patel: Any gotchas with quantized vectors and Faiss?
09:09 Ethan Park: Faiss has PQ/OPQ and supports int8/indexing schemes but you need to retrain the index or adjust distance metric. Quantized vectors can change nearest-neighbor characteristics so re-indexing and eval is required.
09:24 Priya Nair: Good to know.
09:27 Maya Chen: We should probably talk about monitoring — you'll want token-level breakdowns and route-level SLO dashboards. The Redwood Console exposes per-route p50/p95/p99 and token cost breakdowns. You can also hook tracing into your app.
09:44 Priya Nair: Do you export to our Grafana?
09:46 Ethan Park: Yes, we have Prometheus metrics exporters and a Grafana dashboard template. We'll share the stack.
09:52 Priya Nair: Security quick check — SOC2, encryption at rest, KMS?
09:56 Maya Chen: Redwood is SOC 2 compliant, supports customer-managed KMS for Private deployments, and audit logs are available; the security pack will have the certs and details.
10:08 Luca Marino: Timeline — if we sign pilot next week how fast to spin up private nodes?
10:13 Maya Chen: For VPC private deploys it's typically 3-5 business days to provision nodes and connect to your VPC, depending on approvals. On-prem is longer. We'll have a solutions engineer guide you.
10:24 Priya Nair: Ok next steps?
10:27 Maya Chen: Recap — Redwood to share: 1) benchmark spreadsheet and config templates, 2) security packet and SOC2 docs, 3) pilot playbook with scripts, 4) estimate for dedicated pool costs. Dovetail to: confirm pilot sample rate and provide eval queries.
10:47 Priya Nair: We'll aim to get eval set and initial 1% sampling plan by Friday.
10:53 Maya Chen: Great. Any final Qs?
10:56 Samir Patel: One small thing — can you include A100/H100 perf notes? We have access to H100 in one region.
11:03 Ethan Park: We'll add H100 numbers; H100 typically improves throughput and reduces p99 substantially for larger batches. We'll annotate the spreadsheet with GPU assumptions.
11:14 Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and a calendar invite for kickoff.
11:22 Meeting ended.
